doc.title: Pierre Boussaguet interviewed by Matthieu Jaffre, Aix en Provence, France, July 28, 2020

title: Guy Lafitte's last recording and the ballad Charme
summary: Lafitte, weeks from death, is persuaded to come to the studio and records the ballad Charme with his poem.

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: Okay. And in one tune you’re performing also with a great tenor saxophonist Guy Lafitte, before he just passed away a few months later.
A few weeks later. Wow. So you were like the last?
He didn’t want — he was already very sick at home. He knew that he had just a few weeks.
You can’t hear it, that he was sick, on the record.

And what happened is that the night before I called him another time and said, “Guy, come to the studio tomorrow.” And I remember he yelled at me on the phone but like he was crying. He said, “You don’t understand that, I can’t play, it’s been two months, I can’t blow one tune.” And for some reason I said —

He was too fragile to even — and I remember telling him it takes some guts. But of course, I said, “You know what? Forget about the saxophone. But why you don’t pass through the studio and say good-bye to your friends?” And then I said, “Why don’t you write a text, some poetry.” Because he was very gifted about that. And he said, “What kind of poetry?” I said, “Anything, a text, if you have something, and come to say hello to us.” And so he said, he called me back maybe ten or half an hour, he said, “I’ll be there tomorrow.” He grabbed the saxophone. He had a wonderful text that I decided to put on

that piece of music, the ballad called “Charme.” Actually when I wrote the music, those weeks, I wanted to make a reunion of Guy Lafitte and Johnny Griffin. Because they knew each other since ever. But they never played together or just one concert, something like that. And then of course Guy got sick like early April I would say. And so, but I had written that ballad. The original title was “Griff and Guy.” Like Griffin and Guy. G and G. And then I asked Guy, with his beautiful poetry, which the text is a metaphor about how to describe the life of one note. And then he said, “I should try the saxophone.” And he did it. That one track. Then we tried another track and he couldn’t.
But he performed it very well. I mean we can really feel his emotions.
And I’m so glad at that point on the phone, not being shy.
I had to insist but I don’t know, I know what to say, that in some ways it was one more time that little voice that told me it’s the moment to push a little bit.
